name: Neurodiversity
what: This subtopic explores neurodiversity as an overarching concept describing normal variation in brain development, and examines three specific neurodivergent conditions in detail: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and Dyslexia. For each condition, brain differences, strengths, challenges, prevalence, and management strategies are covered.
why: Understanding neurodiversity allows students to recognise that variation in brain functioning is a normal feature of human populations, not a defect. It also builds the knowledge needed to support neurodivergent individuals appropriately in educational and professional contexts.

items.title: I can define neurodiversity and neurodivergence and explain the relationship between them
items.what: Neurodiversity is the term used to describe variations in neurological development and functioning within and between groups of people. Neurodivergent refers to individuals who have a variation in neurological development and functioning, such as those diagnosed with ASD, ADHD, or dyslexia. Neurodiversity is the group-level concept; neurodivergent is the individual-level descriptor.
items.why: Precise use of these terms matters. Calling a group 'neurodiverse' and an individual 'neurodivergent' reflects the actual meaning of the terms and avoids inaccurate language. The framework was developed to normalise brain differences and reduce stigma.
items.example: A classroom that includes students with autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and no diagnosed condition has neurodiversity within it. An individual student diagnosed with dyslexia is described as neurodivergent. The classroom is neurodiverse; the student is neurodivergent.

items.title: I can describe the key features, brain differences, strengths, and challenges of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
items.what: ASD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by impaired social interactions, verbal and non-verbal communication difficulties, narrow interests, and repetitive behaviours. Brain differences include a thinner temporal cortex, a thicker frontal cortex, smaller amygdala, and greater brain volume in childhood. Strengths include exceptional attention to detail and high motivation in areas of interest; challenges include difficulty reading facial expressions and distress over minor routine changes.
items.why: ASD presents differently across individuals and across genders, and understanding its neurological basis and functional profile helps students apply knowledge accurately to case study scenarios and real-world support contexts.
items.example: A person with ASD at a speed dating event might demonstrate the strength of superior retention of facts about a topic they are passionate about, sharing detailed knowledge about a specific country they have visited. At the same time, they might find it difficult to maintain eye contact, which is a recognised challenge associated with ASD.

items.title: I can describe the key features, brain differences, strengths, and challenges of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
items.what: ADHD is a neurological condition characterised by persistent inattention or hyperactivity that disrupts social, academic, or occupational functioning. Brain differences include delayed maturation of the cerebral cortex, smaller amygdala and hippocampus, and faster maturation of the motor cortex. Strengths include hyperfocus and creative problem-solving; challenges include time management, staying on topic, impulsivity, and difficulty articulating feelings.
items.why: ADHD is often mischaracterised as simply an inability to pay attention. Understanding hyperfocus and the neurological basis of the condition gives a more accurate picture and helps students avoid common misconceptions when applying the concept to scenarios.
items.example: A student with ADHD might spend three hours completely absorbed in building a detailed model, ignoring calls to dinner (hyperfocus, a strength), but the next morning be unable to spend ten minutes on a homework task they find uninteresting (difficulty sustaining attention on low-interest tasks, a challenge).

items.title: I can describe the key features, brain differences, strengths, and challenges of dyslexia
items.what: Dyslexia is a neurologically based learning difficulty involving severe challenges in reading, spelling, writing words, and sometimes arithmetic. Brain differences include decreased grey matter volume, weaker white matter organisation, hypoactivation of regions responsible for symbol-to-sound processing, and reduced neuroplasticity in left-hemispheric language areas. Strengths include strong memory, spatial awareness, and big-picture thinking; challenges include reading, writing, forming words, and lack of confidence in literacy-based tasks.
items.why: Dyslexia is frequently misunderstood as laziness or low intelligence. Understanding its neurological basis and the genuine strengths associated with it helps students assess scenarios accurately and avoid deficit-only framings of the condition.
items.example: A student with dyslexia might read 'hippocampus' and process it as 'hypothalamus' due to difficulty matching written symbols to sounds (a recognised challenge). The same student might be highly skilled at explaining complex psychological concepts through vivid verbal storytelling (narrative reasoning, a recognised strength).

items.title: I can compare ASD and ADHD in terms of similarities and differences
items.what: ASD and ADHD share some overlapping features, including repetitive behaviours and difficulty adapting to certain environments. However, ASD is primarily characterised by impaired social communication and narrow interests, whereas ADHD is primarily characterised by persistent inattention or hyperactivity. Brain structures differ between the two conditions, even when behavioural symptoms overlap.
items.why: Comorbidity between ASD and ADHD is documented, and the conditions share surface-level similarities that can lead to diagnostic confusion. Being able to distinguish between them is a key skill for applying psychological knowledge to case studies.
items.example: Both a person with ASD and a person with ADHD might engage in repetitive behaviour, but for different reasons. The person with ASD may repeat an action as part of a narrow, highly specific interest. The person with ADHD may repeat an action because of impulsivity or restlessness, not because of a focused interest.

items.title: I can identify management strategies for ASD, ADHD, and dyslexia
items.what: ASD can be managed through behavioural therapy, speech and occupational therapy, educational support, and medication for accompanying mental health conditions. ADHD can be managed through medication, counselling, and behavioural strategies such as decluttering, designating zones, using planners, and working in small increments. Dyslexia can be managed through audio or video learning, assistive text-to-speech technology, and occupational therapy.
items.why: Knowing management strategies is directly assessed in VCE Psychology and is relevant to real-world support contexts. Management is most effective when tailored to the individual's specific profile and implemented as early as possible.
items.example: A student with ADHD who struggles to focus during a maths lesson might benefit from their teacher implementing behavioural strategies: clearing their desk of unnecessary items (decluttering), working on one problem at a time with a short break after each (working in small increments), and using a visual planner to track which tasks have been completed.
